On Saturday, March 30, 2019 at 1:05:57 PM UTC-5, Eric Rexstad wrote:

> Nicole
>
> Several issues here:
>
> Covered area:  you cannot explicitly specify it.  It incorporates the number of times the point is visited; so it is covered area * number of visits.  Note also that covered area is measured in the same units that distances were measured in (metres?) while Area is measured in whatever units you used; the ds() function does not check for consistency in measurement units; that's the users' responsibility.
> Truncation distance:  model selection tools (AIC) are not useful in determining truncation distance.  It is a subjective decision based upon an assessment of the distance beyond which detections are not providing useful information about the decay of the detection process (the process you are trying to model with the detection function.
> Sense checks of P_a estimates: while your estimates of P_a might be sensible (0.10-0.22)--you must be the judge of whether there are 5-10 birds for each one you detected.  Note however, that for your model with lowest AIC (observer as covariate), the SE(P_a) is enormous--sometime >1.0  That must be wrong.  If you dig into your results for models with observer as covariate, you will see the parameter estimates for these models are non-identifiable.  Specifically the coefficient associated with Observer "R" and Observer "J" have SEs that are really large.  I suspect those two observers had too few detections to do a good job of estimating the nature of their detection function.

Thanks in advance for your advice.

Deanna Leonard

use in your detection function.

release of Distance for Windows).

It is not normal to get different density estimates from different versions of Distance.  We test the releases to check that new versions give the same estimates before release.

messages.subject: dsm model selection with REML
messages.subject_clean: dsm model selection with REML
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance Samplers,

I've got a question about model selection with dsm models that I need to make sure about.

I am fitting a model similar to:

m1 <- dsm(abundance.est ~  s(DEPTH, bs="tp", k = 8),
                              s(COAST, bs=" tp ", k = 8),
                              s(ICE,   bs=" tp ", k = 8),
                            ddf.obj=ddfmodel,
                            segment.data = segdata,
                            observation.data=obsdata,
                            convert.units = 1/1000,
                            availability = 0.8,
                            select = T,
                            gamma = 1,
                            family=nb (), method="REML")

mgcv has two ways to penalize the null space. Here I use “select = T” as a double penalty approach that allows variable selection (within a model) in a single step.
I want to use REML to select the smoothness.

However, I would also like to compare the above model to another model where I replace some of the explanatory variables by other variables that are correlated to them. For instance, I may have a variable SHELF that is correlated with DEPTH. Therefore I do not include both these variables in the same model. But I would like to run m2, where I replace DEPTH by SHELF.

m2 <- dsm(abundance.est ~  s(SHELF, bs="tp", k = 8),
                              s(COAST, bs="tp", k = 8),
                              s(ICE,   bs="tp", k = 8),
                            ddf.obj=ddfmodel,
                            segment.data = segdata,
                            observation.data=obsdata,
                            convert.units = 1/1000,
                            availability = 0.8,
                            select = T,
                            gamma = 1,
                            family=nb(), method="REML")

How can I do model selection between m1 and m2?

1) Can I use AIC do model selection IF I penalise all terms? (even though the models (m1 and m2) I specify do not have the same fixed effects and I use REML?)

2) If AIC is valid, what options do I have if I were to use “family = quasipoisson”, where AIC is not available as far as I know?

3) REML scores should not be used to compare models with different fixed effects structures (Simon Wood; mgcv) – is this still the case when using “select = T”?

4) I do not actually know how to rank models based on their REML scores. Could someone please give me a few pointers (or a good reference to consult)?

Any other practical advice with regards to model selection is also very welcome.

With thanks!
Chris

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] dsm model selection with REML
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] dsm model selection with REML
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris, hi listfolks,

To your questions:

1. AIC model selection is always possible via the AIC() function now
(see Wood, Pya and Säfken, 2016). (The AIC calculated is "right" no
matter how the model is formulated.)

2. Within the quasipoisson response, you could compare REML scores, but
only if all terms in the model are penalized (either by using
select=TRUE or bs="ts") and fixed effects are the same between comparisons.

3. Yes.

4. If by "rank" you mean "do model selection" (as opposed to "order"),
there are no rules of thumb as with AIC, as far as I know. You would
simply have to select the model with the best REML score.

Depending on what you want to do with your model (and how much data you
have), you may be better off thinking about using some cross-validation
strategy to see which of your model provides more generalizable answers
(see, e.g., this paper
https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13107).
Another approach would be to provide some kind of sensitivity analysis
showing whether there are differences in predictions/variance estimates
between the two models (if there are few differences, then maybe it
doesn't matter which model you pick), if you are interested in abundance
estimates.

Hope this helps.

--dave

messages.subject: Changing digital elevation model resolution post-survey?
messages.subject_clean: Changing digital elevation model resolution post-survey?
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm relatively new to distance sampling but this coming year I plan to conduct a small (3-colony) pilot study to test its application in surveying our storm-petrel colonies (sighting burrows then confirming their contents). The colonies are mixed, with both Leach's and fork-tailed storm-petrels breeding sympatrically. Most of the colonies occur on small, tree-covered islets less than 5 ha in size, many colonies cover the entire vegetated portion of the island, and densities may be as high as 4 burrows/m2. We plan to record and treat habitat type as a covariate, but also expect habitat on each individual island to be fairly homogeneous. Many of the islets are remote and haven't been surveyed or even visited in 30-40 years but the hope is to resurvey at least 20 colonies over the next few years.

My main concern (at this point) is the use of digital elevation models. For all islands we have available 20mx20m resolution DEMs that we hope to use to plan the number, length, and location of transects. This would allow us to survey each island with only a single visit. However, we would also like as accurate an estimate of surface area as possible (esp given our expected densities) and could potentially deploy a drone when in the field to create a much more accurate 1mx1m DEM post-survey. Is it possible to use a coarse-scale DEM to plan the location and number of survey transects, then use a finer-scale DEM to estimate colony surface area post-survey? Would creating the 1mx1m DEM prior to survey be worth the extra logistical cost and complication (admittedly hard to estimate at this point)? Any thoughts or advice would be much appreciated!

Many thanks,
Greg

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Changing digital elevation model resolution post-survey?
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Changing digital elevation model resolution post-survey?
messages.body_plain:
Greg

I've not used a DEM to design a distance sampling survey except in the situation where I wanted to have a survey that stratified by elevation--hence the DEM provided information about the strata.

I know nothing about islands where storm petrels breed, but if they are <5ha, I'm guessing the elevation differences might not be large?  Is there high amounts of relief on the island; with some portions of the island being "non habitat" from the birds' perspective or "not surveyable" from the observers' perspective?  That would serve to define my study area as the region about which I am able to make inference. Those would be the reasons I might use DEM information.

Otherwise, I would be tempted not to use DEM data in design of my survey.  I need more context to understand your comment about colony "surface area".  Seems the simple approach is to design a survey such that it covers the entire island, rather than attempt to delineate a colony area.  This way, inference is being made to the island, rather than the colony.  Particularly in the situation you describe, where you intend to make temporal inference about islands visited infrequently, there may be less temporal shift in the size of the island than in the size of the colony (that perhaps shrinks/expands with time).

Regarding the very fine DEM, I would not think information with that detail would be needed prior to the pilot study.  As you can tell my grasp of your sampling situation is a bit weak.  If what I have said is rubbish, you can enlighten me.

You might also want to look at this paper

Jonathan M. Stober, Rocio Prieto-Gonzalez, Lora L. Smith, Tiago A. Marques, and Len Thomas (2017) Techniques for Estimating the Size of Low-Density Gopher Tortoise Populations. Journal of Fish and Wildlife Management: December 2017, Vol. 8, No. 2, pp. 377-386.https://doi.org/10.3996/012017-JFWM-005

that discusses incorporating information on estimated burrow occupancy (and uncertainty) into studies of burrowing animals such as your target species.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] How does Distance software calculate effort?
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] How does Distance software calculate effort?
messages.body_plain:
H.M.

While waiting for more details regarding your question, I manufactured a post-stratification example of my own.  My example is based upon an exercise in Chapter 5 of our online workshop material; where the post-stratification field is group size category.  You can find the Distance project here:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/distance projects/Ch5/Cluster exercise.zip

The details of the survey effort are as follows:

25 line transects with a total length of 1842.8km and 88 detections.

The field 'cluster strat' in the Observation layer divides the 88 observations into three categories (strata): observations of a single individual (39 detections), observations of groups of size 2 (33 detections), and observations of groups of size 3 or more (16 detections).

When post-stratification is employed, detections from (perhaps) more than one stratum might occur on a single transect; e.g. in this data set, transect 1 had 6 detections: 2 of size 1, 2 of size 2 and 3 of size 3 or more.  The confusing point becomes--what effort should be allocated to the each stratum?

Distance actually uses the total effort (1842.8km) to compute encounter rate and subsequent density.  This can be seen on the 'Estimation Summary' page near the end of the program output:

                         Estimate      %CV     df     95% Confidence Interval
                        ------------------------------------------------------
 Stratum:  1
                 n       39.000
                 k       25.000
                 L       1842.8
                 n/L    0.21164E-01   23.72    24.00 0.13057E-01  0.34302E-01
                 Left    0.0000
                 Width   1.5000
 Stratum:  2
                 n       33.000
                 k       25.000
                 L       1842.8
                 n/L    0.17908E-01   30.01    24.00 0.97691E-02  0.32826E-01
                 Left    0.0000
                 Width   1.5000
 Stratum:  3
                 n       16.000
                 k       25.000
                 L       1842.8
                 n/L    0.86825E-02   37.45    24.00 0.41109E-02  0.18338E-01
                 Left    0.0000
                 Width   1.5000

Note that 'n' for each stratum matches the number of detections of the different sizes I described earlier.  Note also that the encounter rates (n/L) are correct for each stratum:  39/1842.8=0.02116345.  This correct encounter rate propagates into the stratum-specific density estimates.

The confusion might arise when contrasting the information from the 'Estimation Summary' above (where effort is correct both in total km of effort and number of transects) with this table at the top of the 'Parameter Estimates' page:

 Effort        :    5528.369
 # samples     :    75
 Width         :    1.500000
 Left          :       0.0000000
 # observations:    88

You will see in this summary that km of effort as well as number of transects is *triple* the correct values.  This is an artefact of there being 3 strata used for the post-stratification.  Distance naively allocates all effort to each of the three post-hoc strata (because effort cannot correctly be allocated to the strata, as the strata were unknown at the time the survey was designed); this equally allocated effort was summed--producing the erroneous values reported on the 'Parameter Estimates' page. Fear not, your encounter rate and density estimates are correct (as shown above).  The values reported on the 'Parameter Estimates' page are incorrect, but are not involved in the final calculations.

Perhaps this is the basis of your question, and I hope it helps answer your question.

> Note that 'n' for each stratum matches the number of detections of the different sizes I described earlier.  Note also that the encounter rates (n/L) are correct for each stratum:  39/1842.8=0.02116345.  This correct encounter rate propagates into the stratum-specific density estimates.
>
> The confusion might arise when contrasting the information from the 'Estimation Summary' above (where effort is correct both in total km of effort and number of transects) with this table at the top of the 'Parameter Estimates' page:
>
>  Effort        :    5528.369
>  # samples     :    75
>  Width         :    1.500000
>  Left          :       0.0000000
>  # observations:    88
>
> You will see in this summary that km of effort as well as number of transects is *triple* the correct values.  This is an artefact of there being 3 strata used for the post-stratification.  Distance naively allocates all effort to each of the three post-hoc strata (because effort cannot correctly be allocated to the strata, as the strata were unknown at the time the survey was designed); this equally allocated effort was summed--producing the erroneous values reported on the 'Parameter Estimates' page. Fear not, your encounter rate and density estimates are correct (as shown above).  The values reported on the 'Parameter Estimates' page are incorrect, but are not involved in the final calculations.
>
> Perhaps this is the basis of your question, and I hope it helps answer your question.
> On 17/04/2019 21:58, hmfost...@gmail.com wrote:

> > Hello,
> >
> > I was wondering how the windows software distance calculates total effort and effort per strata? It keeps overestimating my effort when i post-stratify my data and was just wondering if anyone has any tips/tricks/hints on how to avoid that? Is it the way I import the data? The way the data is organized? My dataset is large so I dont want to upload it. If you need more information about the situation please let me know, but I'm just looking for general tips/suggestions on how to deal with distance calculating effort correctly based on various levels of post-stratification.
> >
> > Thank you!!

messages.body_plain:
Gajanan

I've re-read your earlier question and hopes this explanation helps.  It would help if you confirm that you are performing your analysis using Distance for Windows, as this is the premise of my answer.

If the user chooses to use cluster size as a covariate in the detection function (with the MCDS engine in Distance for Windows), then when switching to the cluster size tab for the model definition, the user is presented with this message:

Continuing with the analysis (noting that size bias regression cannot be conducted when cluster size is a covariate); Distance produces this result:

 Mean cluster size     =   2.2500     Standard error    =  0.22872

 Expected cluster size =   1.9785     Standard error    =      0.00000

 Expected cluster size estimated as the ratio of the estimates of
 density of individuals and density of clusters.

 Note: An estimate of the standard error of the expected cluster
       size is not available because bootstrap options were not
       selected.

You will see the message describing how estimated cluster size is calculated. Following the advice of the message above and using a bootstrap to calculate variance of the estimates, Distance produces:

                         Estimate      %CV     df     95% Confidence Interval
                        ------------------------------------------------------
 Average cluster size
                         2.2500       10.54    88.00     0.00000      0.00000
 Expected cluster size
                         1.9785       11.92           1.5675       2.4974

 Expected cluster size estimated as the ratio of the estimates of density
 of individuals and density of clusters.

 Note: The CV of the expected cluster size was obtained via the bootstrap.

Does that help you to understand how expected cluster size is computed when using cluster size as a covariate?

On 22/04/2019 10:08, Gajanan G Patil wrote:

> I am till confused, If in MCDS regression model may not fit to log(Size) to detection function. Then expected value computed by Sum(Si/Pi), Si=Size and Pi= Pro. detection.????
>
> On Monday, April 15, 2019 at 2:27:35 AM UTC-7, Eric Rexstad wrote:
> >
> > Gajanan
> >
> > A good question.  Have a look at the answer to a similar question I provided on 12Oct18 found on the Google list
> >
> > https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/distance-sampling/JXZft79C__c
> >
> > The short answer to your question is that Distance in R uses a Horwitz-Thompson-like estimator to estimate abundance.  The "Expected cluster size" reported by Distance in R is actually the ratio of the estimated individual abundance divided by the estimated abundance of groups.  You could have a look at the documentation for the function `dht` in the package `mrds` in R help for a bit more detail.
> >
> > Hope that answer is useful.
> > On 15/04/2019 10:09, Gajanan G Patil wrote:
